label: problem:minimal_solomon
title: Problem
body_md:
\label{problem:minimal_solomon}
Is every foliation of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, $n\leq 7$, by properly embedded minimal hypersurfaces a foliation by parallel affine hyperplanes?
head: environment

label: conjecture:cmc_solomon
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{conjecture:cmc_solomon}
Every foliation of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, $n\leq 7$, by (possibly varying) CMC hypersurfaces is a foliation by parallel affine hyperplanes.
head: environment

label: conjecture:yau-docarmo-solomon
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{conjecture:yau-docarmo-solomon}
Every foliation of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ by (possibly varying) CMC hypersurfaces is a foliation by minimal hypersurfaces.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
{\ref*{thm:main_euclidean}}
Let $\mathfrak{F}$ be a codimension one CMC foliation of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. Then, each leaf of $\mathfrak{F}$ is a minimal and stable hypersurface.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
{\ref*{thm:main_euclidean_low_dim}}
Let $\mathfrak{F}$ be a codimension one CMC foliation of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. If $n\leq 6$, then $\mathfrak{F}$ consists entirely of parallel hyperplanes.
head: environment

label: lem:gradH
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:gradH}
$\nabla H=gN$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\mathfrak{F}$ is a CMC foliation, $H$ is constant along each leaf. Hence, \(X(H)=\langle
abla H,Xangle=0\) for every vector field \(X\) tangent to the leaves. Therefore, \(
abla H\) is orthogonal to the leaves and thus parallel to \(N\). Since \(\langle
abla H,Nangle=N(H)=g\) and \(|N|=1\), we conclude that \(
abla H=gN\).
head: environment

label: lem:gT
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:gT}
For every vector field $X$ tangent to a leaf $L$ of $\mathfrak F$, we have
\[
X(g)=g\langle T,X\rangle.
\]
Equivalently, the gradient of $g$ along each leaf satisfies
\[
\nabla_L g=gT.
\]
Consequently, $g$ has constant sign on each leaf $L$: either
$g\equiv0$ on $L$, or $g>0$ everywhere on $L$, or $g<0$
everywhere on $L$.
head: environment

label: lem:divT
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:divT}
$\operatorname{div} T=|A|^2-ng$.
head: environment

label: lem:divX
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: lem:lapL
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\}$ be a local orthonormal frame of $TL$.
By the definition of the Laplace--Beltrami operator on $L$,
$$
\Delta_L f
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(
e_i(e_i f)-(\nabla^L_{e_i}e_i)(f)
\right),
$$
where $\nabla^L$ denotes the Levi-Civita connection of the induced
metric on $L$. On the other hand, the ambient Hessian satisfies
$$
\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i)=e_i(e_i f)-(\nabla_{e_i}e_i)(f),
$$
where $\nabla$ is the Euclidean connection of $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. Since $\nabla_{e_i}e_i$ decomposes into its tangential and normal
components, we have
$$
\nabla_{e_i}e_i=\nabla^L_{e_i}e_i+\langle\nabla_{e_i}e_i,N\rangle N.
$$
Differentiating $\langle e_i,N\rangle=0$ along $e_i$, we obtain
$$
\langle\nabla_{e_i}e_i,N\rangle=-\langle e_i,\nabla_{e_i}N\rangle=\langle Ae_i,e_i\rangle,
$$
where $A(X)=-\nabla_XN$ is the shape operator. Consequently,
$$
\nabla_{e_i}e_i=\nabla^L_{e_i}e_i+\langle Ae_i,e_i\rangle N.
$$
It follows that
\begin{equation}
e_i(e_i f)-(\nabla^L_{e_i}e_i)(f)=\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i)+\langle Ae_i,e_i\rangle N(f).
\end{equation}
Summing over $i$, we get

\begin{eqnarray*}
\Delta_L f & = & \sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i)+\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\langle Ae_i,e_i\rangle\right)N(f)\\
& = & \operatorname{tr}_{TL}\operatorname{Hess}f
+nH\,N(f),    
\end{eqnarray*}
where we used the equation $\operatorname{tr}(A|_{TL})=nH$ (see Equation \eqref{eqtraco}). This proves the Equation \eqref{eq:lapL}.


We now compute the gradient and the Hessian of
$$
\rho(x):=\sqrt{1+|x|^2},
\qquad x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{n+1})\in\mathbb R^{n+1}.
$$

By the chain rule, for every $i=1,\ldots,n+1$, we have $\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial x_i} =\frac{x_i}{\rho}$, and thus
$$
\nabla\rho=\frac{x}{\rho}.
$$
Moreover,
\[
\frac{\partial^2\rho}{\partial x_i\partial x_j}
=
\frac{\delta_{ij}}{\rho}
-\frac{x_ix_j}{\rho^3}.
\]
Hence, the Hessian matrix is
\[
\operatorname{Hess}\rho
=
\frac1\rho I-\frac1{\rho^3}x\otimes x,
\]
where $I$ denotes the identity operator and $x\otimes x$ is the linear
operator defined by
\[
(x\otimes x)(v)=\langle x,v\rangle x,
\qquad v\in\mathbb R^{n+1}.
\]
Equivalently, for any $v,w\in\mathbb R^{n+1}$,
\[
\operatorname{Hess}\rho(v,w)
=
\frac{\langle v,w\rangle}{\rho}
-
\frac{\langle x,v\rangle\langle x,w\rangle}{\rho^3}.
\]
In particular,
\[
\operatorname{Hess}\rho(v,v)
=
\frac{|v|^2}{\rho}
-
\frac{\langle x,v\rangle^2}{\rho^3}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Hess}\rho(v,v)
&\ge
\left(\frac{1}{\rho}-\frac{|x|^2}{\rho^3}\right)|v|^2\\
&=\frac{\rho^2-|x|^2}{\rho^3}|v|^2\\
&=\frac{1}{\rho^3}|v|^2\ge0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Moreover, since $\rho\ge1$, we have
\[
\operatorname{Hess}\rho(v,v)
\le \frac{|v|^2}{\rho}
\le |v|^2.
\]
Hence, in the sense of quadratic forms,
\[
0\le\operatorname{Hess}\rho\le I.
\]
Taking the trace over an orthonormal basis
$\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\}$ of $TL$, we obtain
\[
\operatorname{tr}_{TL}\operatorname{Hess}\rho
=
\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Hess}\rho(e_i,e_i)
\le
\sum_{i=1}^n|e_i|^2
=n.
\]
Furthermore,
\[
|N(\rho)|
=
|\langle\nabla\rho,N\rangle|
\le|\nabla\rho|
=
\frac{|x|}{\rho}
\le1.
\]
Applying \eqref{eq:lapL} to $\rho$, we conclude that
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_L\rho
&=
\operatorname{tr}_{TL}\operatorname{Hess}\rho
+nH\,N(\rho)\\
&\le n+n|H|\,|N(\rho)|\\
&\le n(1+|H|).
\end{aligned}
\]
This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: lem:hessian
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:hessian}
Let $\chi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$ and let $q\geq 4$ be an
integer. Then
\[
\operatorname{Hess}(\chi^q)
=
q(q-1)\chi^{q-2}\,d\chi\otimes d\chi
+
q\chi^{q-1}\operatorname{Hess}\chi.
\]
Here, the Hessian is regarded as a symmetric bilinear form, and
$d\chi\otimes d\chi$ denotes the bilinear form defined by
\[
(d\chi\otimes d\chi)(v,w)=d\chi(v)d\chi(w).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $v,w\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ be arbitrary vectors. By the
definition of the Hessian,
\[
\operatorname{Hess}(\chi^q)(v,w)
=
\left\langle
D_v\bigl(\nabla(\chi^q)\bigr),w
\right\rangle.
\]
By the chain rule,
\[
\nabla(\chi^q)=q\chi^{q-1}\nabla\chi.
\]
Differentiating this identity in the direction of $v$ and applying
the product rule, we obtain
\[
D_v\bigl(\nabla(\chi^q)\bigr)
=
q(q-1)\chi^{q-2}d\chi(v)\nabla\chi
+
q\chi^{q-1}D_v(\nabla\chi).
\]
Taking the inner product with $w$ gives
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Hess}(\chi^q)(v,w)
={}&q(q-1)\chi^{q-2}
d\chi(v)\langle\nabla\chi,w\rangle
+q\chi^{q-1}
\langle D_v(\nabla\chi),w\rangle.
\end{align*}
Since
\[
d\chi(w)=\langle\nabla\chi,w\rangle
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{Hess}\chi(v,w)
=
\langle D_v(\nabla\chi),w\rangle,
\]
we conclude that
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Hess}(\chi^q)(v,w)
={}&q(q-1)\chi^{q-2}d\chi(v)d\chi(w)
+q\chi^{q-1}\operatorname{Hess}\chi(v,w).
\end{aligned}
\]
By the definition of $d\chi\otimes d\chi$, this is equivalent to
\[
\operatorname{Hess}(\chi^q)
=
q(q-1)\chi^{q-2}\,d\chi\otimes d\chi
+
q\chi^{q-1}\operatorname{Hess}\chi.
\]
Since $v$ and $w$ were arbitrary, the identity holds everywhere
on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$.
head: environment

label: lem:divV
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $H$, $N$, and $T$ are smooth and $p$ is an integer, the
vector field $V$ defined in \eqref{eq:V} is smooth on
$\mathbb R^{n+1}$. We first compute the divergence of each term in $V$. By the
product rule for the divergence,
\[
\operatorname{div}(H^pN)
=
\langle\nabla(H^p),N\rangle
+H^p\operatorname{div}N.
\]
Using the chain rule and the identities 
$\nabla H=gN$ (see Lemma \ref{lem:gradH}) and $\operatorname{div}N=-nH$, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{div}(H^pN)
&=pH^{p-1}\langle\nabla H,N\rangle
-nH^{p+1}\\
&=pH^{p-1}g\langle N,N\rangle
-nH^{p+1}\\
&=pH^{p-1}g-nH^{p+1},
\end{aligned}
\]
where we used $|N|=1$.

Next, applying the product rule to the second term gives
\[
\operatorname{div}(H^{p-1}T)
=
\langle\nabla(H^{p-1}),T\rangle
+H^{p-1}\operatorname{div}T.
\]
Since
\[
\nabla(H^{p-1})
=(p-1)H^{p-2}\nabla H
=(p-1)H^{p-2}gN
\]
and $T\perp N$, we have
\[
\langle\nabla(H^{p-1}),T\rangle
=(p-1)H^{p-2}g\langle N,T\rangle=0.
\]
Therefore, by Lemma~\ref{lem:divT},
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{div}\left(\frac{p}{n}H^{p-1}T\right)
&=\frac{p}{n}H^{p-1}\operatorname{div}T\\
&=\frac{p}{n}H^{p-1}(|A|^2-ng)\\
&=\frac{p}{n}H^{p-1}|A|^2
-pH^{p-1}g.
\end{aligned}
\]

Adding the two divergence identities, we find that
$$
\operatorname{div}V=pH^{p-1}g-nH^{p+1}+\frac{p}{n}H^{p-1}|A|^2-pH^{p-1}g=\frac{p}{n}H^{p-1}|A|^2-nH^{p+1}.
$$
Thus, the terms involving $g$ cancel identically, and the
equality in \eqref{eq:divV} follows without any assumption on
the signs of $g$ or $H$.

It remains to establish the inequality. By the
Cauchy--Schwarz inequality,
\[
\bigl(\operatorname{tr}(A|_{TL})\bigr)^2
\le n\,|A|^2.
\]
Since $\operatorname{tr}(A|_{TL})=nH$, this yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:CS}
|A|^2\ge nH^2.
\end{equation}
Because $p$ is odd, $p-1$ is even, and hence
$H^{p-1}\ge0$. Multiplying \eqref{eq:CS} by
$\frac{p}{n}H^{p-1}\ge0$, we obtain
\[
\frac{p}{n}H^{p-1}|A|^2
\ge pH^{p+1}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{div}V
&=\frac{p}{n}H^{p-1}|A|^2-nH^{p+1}\\
&\ge pH^{p+1}-nH^{p+1}\\
&=(p-n)H^{p+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Finally, since $p+1$ is even,
\[
H^{p+1}=|H|^{p+1}.
\]
Moreover, $p>n$ implies $p-n>0$. Therefore,
\[
\operatorname{div}V
\ge(p-n)|H|^{p+1}\ge0,
\]
which completes the proof.
head: environment

label: lem:T
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:T}
Let $\chi\in C^\infty_c(\mathbb R^{n+1})$ and let
$\kappa\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^{n+1})$ be constant along the
leaves of the foliation. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:T}
\begin{aligned}
\kappa\langle\nabla\chi,T\rangle
={}&\kappa\,\operatorname{tr}_{TL}\operatorname{Hess}\chi
+nH\kappa\,N(\chi)
-\operatorname{div}(\kappa\nabla_L\chi),
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where
\[
\nabla_L\chi:=\nabla\chi-N(\chi)N
\]
is the leafwise gradient of $\chi$. In particular,
$\kappa\nabla_L\chi$ is a smooth compactly supported vector
field on $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ tangent to the leaves, and
\[
\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}
\operatorname{div}(\kappa\nabla_L\chi)\,d x=0.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first observe that
\[
\nabla_L\chi=\nabla\chi-N(\chi)N
\]
is the orthogonal projection of $\nabla\chi$ onto the tangent
space of each leaf. In particular,
$
\langle\nabla_L\chi,N\rangle=0.
$
Since $T$ is tangent to the leaves, we also have
\[
\langle\nabla\chi,T\rangle
=
\langle\nabla_L\chi,T\rangle.
\]
On each leaf $L$, the restriction of $\nabla_L\chi$ is the
intrinsic gradient of $\chi|_L$. Therefore,
\[
\operatorname{div}_L(\nabla_L\chi)=\Delta_L\chi.
\]
Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:divX} to the tangential vector field
$X=\nabla_L\chi$, we obtain
\[
\operatorname{div}(\nabla_L\chi)
=
\operatorname{div}_L(\nabla_L\chi)
-\langle\nabla_L\chi,T\rangle.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\langle\nabla_L\chi,T\rangle
=
\Delta_L\chi-\operatorname{div}(\nabla_L\chi).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\langle\nabla\chi,T\rangle
=
\Delta_L\chi-\operatorname{div}(\nabla_L\chi).
\]

By Lemma~\ref{lem:lapL}, the intrinsic Laplacian satisfies
\[
\Delta_L\chi
=
\operatorname{tr}_{TL}\operatorname{Hess}\chi
+nH\,N(\chi).
\]
Substituting this identity, we conclude that
\[
\begin{aligned}
\langle\nabla\chi,T\rangle
={}&\operatorname{tr}_{TL}\operatorname{Hess}\chi
+nH\,N(\chi)
-\operatorname{div}(\nabla_L\chi).
\end{aligned}
\]

Multiplying by $\kappa$, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\kappa\langle\nabla\chi,T\rangle
={}&\kappa\,\operatorname{tr}_{TL}\operatorname{Hess}\chi
+nH\kappa\,N(\chi)-\kappa\operatorname{div}(\nabla_L\chi).
\end{aligned}
\]

It remains to rewrite the last term. By the product rule
for the divergence,
\[
\operatorname{div}(\kappa\nabla_L\chi)
=
\langle\nabla\kappa,\nabla_L\chi\rangle
+\kappa\operatorname{div}(\nabla_L\chi).
\]
Since $\kappa$ is constant along the leaves, its derivative
in every tangential direction vanishes. Thus,
\[
\langle\nabla\kappa,X\rangle=0
\qquad\text{for every }X\in TL.
\]
Equivalently, $\nabla\kappa$ is parallel to $N$. Because
$\nabla_L\chi$ is tangent to the leaves, it follows that
\[
\langle\nabla\kappa,\nabla_L\chi\rangle=0.
\]
Hence,
\[
\operatorname{div}(\kappa\nabla_L\chi)
=
\kappa\operatorname{div}(\nabla_L\chi).
\]
Substituting this equality into the preceding expression
gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\kappa\langle\nabla\chi,T\rangle
={}&\kappa\,\operatorname{tr}_{TL}\operatorname{Hess}\chi
+nH\kappa\,N(\chi)-\operatorname{div}(\kappa\nabla_L\chi),
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:T}.

Finally, since $\chi$ is compactly supported and
$\nabla_L\chi$ is obtained from $\nabla\chi$ by orthogonal
projection, $\nabla_L\chi$ is also compactly supported.
Multiplication by the smooth function $\kappa$ preserves
compact support. Thus $\kappa\nabla_L\chi$ is a smooth
compactly supported vector field on $\mathbb R^{n+1}$.
The divergence theorem, applied on a sufficiently large
ball containing its support, yields
\[
\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}
\operatorname{div}(\kappa\nabla_L\chi)\,dx=0.
\]
This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: prop:int
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: eq:integraldivW
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\chi\in C^\infty_c(\mathbb R^{n+1})$ and recall that
$q=p+1$. Consider the vector field
\[
W:=\chi^qV,
\]
where
$
V=H^pN+\frac{p}{n}H^{p-1}T
$
is the smooth vector field defined in Lemma~\ref{lem:divV}.
Since $\chi$ has compact support, $W$ is a smooth compactly
supported vector field on $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. Hence, by the
divergence theorem,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:integraldivW}
\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}\operatorname{div}W=0.
\end{equation}

By the product rule for the divergence,
\[
\operatorname{div}W
=
\chi^q\operatorname{div}V
+\langle\nabla(\chi^q),V\rangle.
\]
Using the definition of $V$, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{div}W
={}&\chi^q\operatorname{div}V
+H^pN(\chi^q)+\frac{p}{n}H^{p-1}
\langle\nabla(\chi^q),T\rangle.
\end{aligned}
\]

We now apply Lemma~\ref{lem:T} with the test function $\chi^q$
and the function
\[
\kappa:=\frac{p}{n}H^{p-1}.
\]
The function $\kappa$ is smooth and constant along the leaves,
because $H$ is constant on each leaf. Thus, Lemma~\ref{lem:T}
gives

\begin{equation*}
\frac{p}{n}H^{p-1}
\langle\nabla(\chi^q),T\rangle  =  \frac{p}{n}H^{p-1}
\operatorname{tr}_{TL}\operatorname{Hess}(\chi^q)
+pH^pN(\chi^q)-
\operatorname{div}\left(
\frac{p}{n}H^{p-1}\nabla_L(\chi^q)
\right).    
\end{equation*}


Substituting this identity into the expression for
$\operatorname{div}W$, we find

\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{div}W=\chi^q\operatorname{div}V
+(p+1)H^pN(\chi^q)+\frac{p}{n}H^{p-1}
\operatorname{tr}_{TL}\operatorname{Hess}(\chi^q)-\operatorname{div}\left(
\frac{p}{n}H^{p-1}\nabla_L(\chi^q)
\right).    
\end{equation*}
    




Integrating over $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, the divergence theorem
and the compact support of $\chi$ imply
\[
\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}
\operatorname{div}\left(
\frac{p}{n}H^{p-1}\nabla_L(\chi^q)
\right)=0.
\]
Together with \eqref{eq:integraldivW}, this yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intid}
\begin{aligned}
\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}\chi^q\operatorname{div}V
={}&-(p+1)\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}H^pN(\chi^q)-\frac{p}{n}\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}
H^{p-1}\operatorname{tr}_{TL}
\operatorname{Hess}(\chi^q).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

We next estimate both sides of \eqref{eq:intid}. Since $q$ is
even, $\chi^q\ge0$. Therefore, by inequality \eqref{eq:divV} in Lemma~\ref{lem:divV} implies
\[
\begin{aligned}
(p-n)\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}\chi^qH^{p+1}
&\le
\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}\chi^q\operatorname{div}V.
\end{aligned}
\]
Combining this inequality with \eqref{eq:intid}, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(p-n)\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}\chi^qH^{p+1} \le
-(p+1)\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}H^pN(\chi^q)-\frac{p}{n}\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}
H^{p-1}\operatorname{tr}_{TL}
\operatorname{Hess}(\chi^q).
\end{aligned}
\]

To estimate the first integral on the right-hand side, we use
the fact that $N$ is a unit vector field. Thus,
\[
|N(\chi^q)|
=
|\langle\nabla(\chi^q),N\rangle|
\le|\nabla(\chi^q)|.
\]
Consequently,
\[
-\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}H^pN(\chi^q)
\le
\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}
|H|^p\,|\nabla(\chi^q)|.
\]

For the second integral, recall that $p-1$ is even, so
$H^{p-1}\ge0$. Moreover, for any symmetric endomorphism $S$
of an $n$-dimensional inner product space,
\[
|\operatorname{tr}S|\le n\|S\|,
\]
where $\|S\|$ denotes the operator norm. Applying this
inequality to the restriction of
$\operatorname{Hess}(\chi^q)$ to $TL$, we obtain
\[
\left|
\operatorname{tr}_{TL}\operatorname{Hess}(\chi^q)
\right|
\le
n\|\operatorname{Hess}(\chi^q)\|.
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
&-\frac{p}{n}\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}
H^{p-1}\operatorname{tr}_{TL}
\operatorname{Hess}(\chi^q)\le
p\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}
H^{p-1}\|\operatorname{Hess}(\chi^q)\|.
\end{aligned}
\]

Combining the preceding estimates, we conclude that
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(p-n)\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}\chi^qH^{p+1}\le
(p+1)\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}
|H|^p\,|\nabla(\chi^q)|+
p\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}
H^{p-1}\|\operatorname{Hess}(\chi^q)\|.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:int}.
head: environment

label: eq:cutoff
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
To prove these estimates, let $x\ne0$ and write
\[
r:=|x|,
\qquad
\widehat{x}:=\frac{x}{r}.
\]
Thus $|\widehat{x}|=1$. Since $r=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}x_i^2\right)^{1/2},$ we have
\[
\frac{\partial r}{\partial x_i}
=
\frac{x_i}{r},
\qquad i=1,\ldots,n+1.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\nabla r=\frac{x}{r}=\widehat{x}.
\]

By the chain rule,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla\chi_R
&=
\chi_0'\left(\frac{r}{R}\right)
\nabla\left(\frac{r}{R}\right)\\
&=
\frac{1}{R}\chi_0'\left(\frac{r}{R}\right)\nabla r\\
&=
\frac{\chi_0'(r/R)}{R}\widehat{x}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since $|\widehat{x}|=1$, it follows that
\[
|\nabla\chi_R|
=
\frac{1}{R}\left|\chi_0'\left(\frac{r}{R}\right)\right|
\le
\frac{\sup_{s\ge0}|\chi_0'(s)|}{R}
\le\frac{C_0}{R}.
\]
This proves the first estimate in \eqref{eq:cutoff}.

We now compute the Hessian. Recall that, for vectors
$u,v\in\mathbb R^{n+1}$, the tensor product $u\otimes v$
defines the linear operator
\[
(u\otimes v)(w):=\langle v,w\rangle u.
\]
In particular,
\[
(\widehat{x}\otimes\widehat{x})(v)
=
\langle\widehat{x},v\rangle\widehat{x}.
\]
Since $|\widehat{x}|=1$, the operator
$\widehat{x}\otimes\widehat{x}$ is the orthogonal projection
onto the radial direction $\operatorname{span}\{\widehat{x}\}$,
whereas
\[
I-\widehat{x}\otimes\widehat{x}
\]
is the orthogonal projection onto the orthogonal complement
$\widehat{x}^{\perp}$. For convenience, define
\[
a(r):=\frac{1}{R}\chi_0'\left(\frac{r}{R}\right).
\]
Then
\[
\nabla\chi_R=a(r)\widehat{x}.
\]
For any $v\in\mathbb R^{n+1}$, the product rule gives
\begin{eqnarray*}
\operatorname{Hess}\chi_R(v)=D(\nabla\chi_R)(v) & = & Da(v)\,\widehat{x}+a(r)D\widehat{x}(v)\\
& = & a'(r)Dr(v)\,\widehat{x}+a(r)D\widehat{x}(v).
\end{eqnarray*}
First, by the chain rule,
\[
a'(r)=\frac{1}{R^2}\chi_0''\left(\frac{r}{R}\right).
\]
Since $Dr(v)=\langle \nabla r,v\rangle =\langle\widehat{x},v\rangle$, we obtain
\[
Da(v)
=
\frac{1}{R^2}\chi_0''\left(\frac{r}{R}\right)
\langle\widehat{x},v\rangle.
\]
Therefore,

\begin{equation}\label{eq.diva}
Da(v)\,\widehat{x}  =  
\frac{1}{R^2}\chi_0''\left(\frac{r}{R}\right)
\langle\widehat{x},v\rangle\widehat{x}\\
= \frac{1}{R^2}\chi_0''\left(\frac{r}{R}\right)
(\widehat{x}\otimes\widehat{x})(v).    
\end{equation}

Next, since $\widehat{x}=x/r$, differentiation in the
direction $v$ yields
\[
D\widehat{x}(v)
=
\frac{v}{r}-\frac{x}{r^2}Dr(v).
\]
Using $x=r\widehat{x}$ and
$Dr(v)=\langle\widehat{x},v\rangle$, we find that
\[
\begin{aligned}
D\widehat{x}(v)
&=
\frac{v}{r}
-\frac{\widehat{x}}{r}
\langle\widehat{x},v\rangle\\
&=
\frac{1}{r}
\left(v-\langle\widehat{x},v\rangle\widehat{x}\right)\\
&=
\frac{1}{r}
\left(I-\widehat{x}\otimes\widehat{x}\right)(v).
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence,
\[
D\widehat{x}
=
\frac{1}{r}
\left(I-\widehat{x}\otimes\widehat{x}\right).
\]
Multiplying by $a(r)$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq.divxchapeu}
a(r)D\widehat{x}
=
\frac{\chi_0'(r/R)}{Rr}
\left(I-\widehat{x}\otimes\widehat{x}\right).    
\end{equation}


Combining the two Equations \eqref{eq.diva} and \eqref{eq.divxchapeu} in the derivative of
$\nabla\chi_R$, we conclude that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hesscutoff}
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Hess}\chi_R
={}&
\frac{\chi_0''(r/R)}{R^2}
\widehat{x}\otimes\widehat{x}+
\frac{\chi_0'(r/R)}{Rr}
\left(I-\widehat{x}\otimes\widehat{x}\right).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

We next estimate the operator norm of this Hessian.
Set
\[
P:=\widehat{x}\otimes\widehat{x},
\qquad
Q:=I-P,
\]
and
\[
\alpha:=\frac{\chi_0''(r/R)}{R^2},
\qquad
\beta:=\frac{\chi_0'(r/R)}{Rr}.
\]
Then \eqref{eq:hesscutoff} becomes
\[
\operatorname{Hess}\chi_R=\alpha P+\beta Q.
\]
The operators $P$ and $Q$ are orthogonal projections onto
complementary orthogonal subspaces. In particular, for every
$v\in\mathbb R^{n+1}$,
\[
v=Pv+Qv,\qquad
\langle Pv,Qv\rangle=0,
\]
and therefore
\[
|v|^2=|Pv|^2+|Qv|^2.
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
|\operatorname{Hess}\chi_R(v)|^2
&=|\alpha Pv+\beta Qv|^2\\
&=\alpha^2|Pv|^2+\beta^2|Qv|^2\\
&\le
\max\{|\alpha|^2,|\beta|^2\}
\left(|Pv|^2+|Qv|^2\right)\\
&=
\max\{|\alpha|^2,|\beta|^2\}|v|^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking the supremum over all unit vectors $v$, we obtain
\[
\|\operatorname{Hess}\chi_R\|
\le\max\{|\alpha|,|\beta|\}.
\]
Equality holds because the radial subspace and its orthogonal
complement are nontrivial eigenspaces of the Hessian. Hence,
\[
\|\operatorname{Hess}\chi_R\|
=
\max\left\{
\frac{|\chi_0''(r/R)|}{R^2},
\frac{|\chi_0'(r/R)|}{Rr}
\right\}.
\]

Finally, since $\chi_0$ is constant on $[0,1]$ and on
$[2,\infty)$, both $\nabla\chi_R$ and
$\operatorname{Hess}\chi_R$ vanish outside the annulus $R\le r\le2R.$ On this annulus, $r\ge R$, so
$\frac{1}{Rr}\le\frac{1}{R^2}.$ Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|\operatorname{Hess}\chi_R\|
&\le
\frac{1}{R^2}
\max\left\{
\sup_{s\ge0}|\chi_0''(s)|,
\sup_{s\ge0}|\chi_0'(s)|
\right\}\\
&\le\frac{C_0}{R^2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves the second estimate in \eqref{eq:cutoff}, and
completes the proof of both claimed bounds.
head: environment

label: thm:main_euclidean
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main_euclidean}
Let $\mathfrak{F}$ be a codimension one CMC foliation of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. Then, each leaf of $\mathfrak{F}$ is a minimal and stable hypersurface.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $R>0$, let $\chi:=\chi_R$, where $\chi_R$ is defined in Subsection \ref{subsec:estimates}, and define
\[
a:=|H|\chi\geq 0.
\]
Recall that $q=p+1$, where $p>n$ is an odd integer. By the estimates in
\eqref{eq:cutoff}, we have
\[
|\nabla\chi|\leq \frac{C_0}{R},
\qquad
\|\operatorname{Hess}\chi\|\leq \frac{C_0}{R^2}.
\]
Since $0\leq\chi\leq 1$, the chain rule yields
\[
\nabla(\chi^q)=q\chi^{q-1}\nabla\chi
=q\chi^p\nabla\chi,
\]
and hence
\[
|\nabla(\chi^q)|
=q\chi^p|\nabla\chi|
\leq \frac{qC_0}{R}\chi^p.
\]

By Lemma \ref{lem:hessian}, we have
\[
\operatorname{Hess}(\chi^q)
=
q(q-1)\chi^{q-2}\,d\chi\otimes d\chi
+
q\chi^{q-1}\operatorname{Hess}\chi.
\]


Taking operator norms and using $q-1=p$ and $q-2=p-1$, we obtain
\begin{align*}
\|\operatorname{Hess}(\chi^q)\|
&\leq q(q-1)\chi^{p-1}|\nabla\chi|^2
+q\chi^p\|\operatorname{Hess}\chi\|\\
&\leq \frac{q(q-1)C_0^2}{R^2}\chi^{p-1}
+\frac{qC_0}{R^2}\chi^p\\
&\leq \frac{C_1}{R^2}\chi^{p-1},
\end{align*}
where $C_1:=q(q-1)C_0^2+qC_0.$ In the last inequality, we used $\chi^p\leq\chi^{p-1}$. Since $p$ is odd, both $p+1$ and $p-1$ are even. Therefore,
\[
|H|^p\chi^p=a^p,
\qquad
H^{p-1}\chi^{p-1}=a^{p-1},
\qquad
\chi^{p+1}H^{p+1}=a^{p+1}.
\]
Moreover, $\chi$ vanishes outside $\overline{B_{2R}}$, and thus
$a$ also vanishes there. Set
\[
I=I(R):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n+1}}\chi^{p+1}H^{p+1}
=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n+1}}a^{p+1}.
\]
In particular, $I<\infty$. Define the constants
\[
A_1:=(p+1)qC_0,
\qquad
A_2:=pC_1.
\]
Applying Proposition~\ref{prop:int} and the preceding estimates, we obtain
\begin{align*}
(p-n)I
&\leq (p+1)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n+1}}
|H|^p|\nabla(\chi^q)|
+p\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n+1}}
H^{p-1}\|\operatorname{Hess}(\chi^q)\|\\
&\leq \frac{A_1}{R}\int_{B_{2R}}a^p
+\frac{A_2}{R^2}\int_{B_{2R}}a^{p-1}.
\end{align*}

Let
\[
\mathcal V:=|B_{2R}|=\omega_{n+1}(2R)^{n+1},
\]
where $\omega_{n+1}$ denotes the volume of the unit ball in
$\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. Since $a\geq0$ and
\[
\int_{B_{2R}}a^{p+1}
\leq \int_{\mathbb{R}^{n+1}}a^{p+1}=I,
\]
H\"older's inequality gives
\begin{align*}
\int_{B_{2R}}a^p
&\leq
\left(\int_{B_{2R}}a^{p+1}\right)^{\frac{p}{p+1}}
|B_{2R}|^{\frac{1}{p+1}}\\
&\leq I^{\frac{p}{p+1}}\mathcal V^{\frac{1}{p+1}},
\end{align*}
and, in the same way,
\begin{align*}
\int_{B_{2R}}a^{p-1}
&\leq
\left(\int_{B_{2R}}a^{p+1}\right)^{\frac{p-1}{p+1}}
|B_{2R}|^{\frac{2}{p+1}}\\
&\leq I^{\frac{p-1}{p+1}}\mathcal V^{\frac{2}{p+1}}.
\end{align*}
Now put
\[
X:=I^{\frac{1}{p+1}},
\qquad
Y:=\frac{\mathcal V^{\frac{1}{p+1}}}{R}.
\]
Both $X$ and $Y$ are nonnegative, and $Y>0$. Substituting the
H\"older estimates into the preceding integral inequality yields
\[
(p-n)X^{p+1}
\leq A_1X^pY+A_2X^{p-1}Y^2.
\]

If $X=0$, then $X\leq\Lambda Y$ holds trivially for every
$\Lambda>0$. Suppose, therefore, that $X>0$. Dividing the last
inequality by $X^{p-1}Y^2>0$, we obtain
\[
(p-n)\left(\frac{X}{Y}\right)^2
-A_1\frac{X}{Y}-A_2\leq0.
\]
Writing $s:=X/Y$, this becomes
\[
(p-n)s^2-A_1s-A_2\leq0.
\]
Since $p-n>0$ and $s\geq0$, the quadratic inequality implies
\[
s\leq
\frac{A_1+\sqrt{A_1^2+4(p-n)A_2}}{2(p-n)}
=:\Lambda.
\]
Consequently, in both cases $X=0$ and $X>0$, we have
\[
X\leq\Lambda Y.
\]
Raising this inequality to the power $p+1$ and recalling the
definitions of $X$ and $Y$, we conclude that
\[
I\leq\Lambda^{p+1}\frac{\mathcal V}{R^{p+1}}.
\]
Since $\mathcal V=\omega_{n+1}(2R)^{n+1}$, it follows that
\[
I(R)\leq
\Lambda^{p+1}\omega_{n+1}2^{n+1}R^{n-p}.
\]
The constant $\Lambda$ depends only on $n$, $p$, and the chosen
cutoff function $\chi_0$. Moreover, since $\chi=1$ on $B_R$ and
$H^{p+1}=|H|^{p+1}\geq0$, we have
\begin{equation*}
\int_{B_R}{|H|^{p+1}}\leq I(R)\leq
\Lambda^{p+1}\omega_{n+1}2^{n+1}R^{n-p}.
\label{eq:decay}
\end{equation*}

We now show that $H$ vanishes identically. Fix $R_0>0$. For every
$R\geq R_0$, the inclusion $B_{R_0}\subset B_R$ and the
nonnegativity of $|H|^{p+1}$ imply
\[
0\leq\int_{B_{R_0}}|H|^{p+1}
\leq\int_{B_R}|H|^{p+1}
\leq
\Lambda^{p+1}\omega_{n+1}2^{n+1}R^{n-p}.
\]
Because $p>n$, we have $n-p<0$, and therefore
\[
\lim_{R\to\infty}R^{n-p}=0.
\]
Letting $R\to\infty$ in the preceding inequality gives
\[
\int_{B_{R_0}}|H|^{p+1}=0.
\]
The function $|H|^{p+1}$ is continuous and nonnegative. Hence it
must vanish at every point of $B_{R_0}$; otherwise, continuity
would give a neighborhood on which it is strictly positive,
contradicting the vanishing of its integral. Thus $H=0$ on $B_{R_0}$. Since $R_0>0$ was arbitrary, we conclude that $H\equiv0$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}.$ Therefore, every leaf of $\mathfrak F$ has vanishing mean curvature and is consequently a minimal hypersurface. Finally, stability follows from Theorem 1 of \cite{Oshikiri-1982}.
head: environment

label: thm:main_euclidean_low_dim
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{thm:main_euclidean_low_dim}
Let $\mathfrak{F}$ be a codimension one CMC foliation of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. If $n\leq 6$, then $\mathfrak{F}$ consists entirely of parallel hyperplanes.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem \ref{thm:main_euclidean}, the leaves are minimal and stable hypersurfaces. 
We know that in an orientable space (e.g. in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$) a hypersurface is orientable if and only if it is two-sided.
Since $\mathfrak{F}$ is transversely oriented, each leaf $L\in \mathfrak{F}$ is oriented. Since $n\leq 6$ and each leaf is a complete, minimal, stable, oriented hypersurface, we have, by the main results in \cite{doCarmoP:1979}, \cite{ColbrieS:1979} (for $n=2$), \cite{ChodoshL-2021} (for $n=3$), \cite{ChodoshLMD-2024} (for $n=4$), \cite{Mazet} (for $n=5$), and \cite{HongLW:2026} (for $n=6$), that each leaf $L$ of the foliation is a hyperplane.
head: environment
